thread.title: A Former CEO of Apple and Pepsi Sets His Sights on Health Care

title: A Former CEO of Apple and Pepsi Sets His Sights on Health Care
text:
A Former CEO of Apple and Pepsi Sets His Sights on Health Care By Oct. 10, 2018 6:30 a.m. ET Order Reprints John Sculley Web Summit Text size
John Sculley made his name as chief executive of Apple (AAPL) and PepsiCo (PEP). Now he wants to make an impact on health care.
Sculley is chairman and chief marketing officer at RxAdvance , a cloud-based platform that helps pharmaceutical companies, hospitals, and insurers manage chronically ill patients living at home. Sculley says RxAdvance will make a dent in the $3.5 trillion health care industry.
In fact, he’s convinced technologies like machine learning, precision medicine, and robotics are capable of redefining health care—or any industry—thrusting it into a digital age of efficiency, cost savings, and data-rich customer profiles.
“We’re in a new world where things move in exponential time, and technology makes it possible,” Sculley tells Barron’s . “There has never been a better time to do things entrepreneurially.”
Sculley, a serial entrepreneur and investor in consumer technology, data management, and telecommunications, says RxAdvance can disrupt the pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) field. Traditional PBMs negotiate lower rates for drugs, but RxAdvance’s use of computing power enables it to manage expenses significantly better, helping health insurance companies tamp down costs, he says.
RxAdvance logged about $500 million in contracted revenue in 2017 and is nearing profitability, says Sculley, who estimates the Boston-based company will reach at least $10 billion in revenue by 2020. In March, health insurer Centene (CNC) made an undisclosed investment in RxAdvance. Newsletter Sign-up
Sculley famously clashed with Apple co-founder Steve Jobs over management styles and product strategy, which led to Jobs’s ouster in 1985. Sculley himself was forced out in 1993 over a dispute about licensing Macintosh software to other PC makers. The board was in favor of such a move and pursued it, with dismal results.
His reign at Apple is a topic nearly everyone asks Sculley about 25 years later.
“I learned that you don’t really understand something well unless you understand it more than one way,” Sculley says. “In the early 1980s, everyone else but Steve Jobs saw the future of computers as business and scientific machines.”
“Steve Jobs looked at the same facts that Moore’s Law would make computers increasingly more powerful, but he also understood that Moore’s Law would also make computer technology so inexpensive that someday everyone could afford to have their own personal computer,” Sculley adds.
Sculley says what took six years to develop at a tech company a decade ago now requires only two. “In tech, you have to adapt quickly, period,” he says.
The blurring speed of the industry, Sculley says, plays to the managerial experience of long-time executives like himself and Meg Whitman, the former CEO of Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) and eBay (EBAY) who now runs a new mobile video startup in Hollywood under the working title of NewTV .
“We can recognize what is big and what it takes to get there from here,” says Sculley, who ran Apple for a decade, from 1983 to 1993, building it into an $8 billion business.
But with speed comes risk. Sculley acknowledges that companies can grow too fast, and suffer “unexpected, unintended consequences.”
“I think social media will experience foundational changes, though I don’t know what it will be,” Sculley says.
